issues: totaling over one hundred volumes → 凡百餘部: over a hundred works (部), not volumes; The Bodhisattva knew … he traveled back and forth three times, yet could not resolve his doubts → 往來三返，不得決疑: it is Guṇaprabha who went back and forth three times; DM's “he” reads as Maitreya (Mizutani: 徳光は往来すること三返; Beal: though he went and returned three times, ambiguous)
en_revised: Four or five li south of the great city, one arrives at a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (known in Chinese as De Guang, "Virtue-Light") composed the *Bian zhen lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Truth) and other works here, over a hundred works in all. As a youth, the master was heroic and outstanding; as he grew older, he became broad-minded and quick-witted, possessing vast knowledge and a retentive memory, and was a scholar of great learning. He originally studied the Mahāyāna, but not having exhausted its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and subsequently abandoned his former studies to learn the Hīnayāna. He composed several dozen treatises to refute the principles of the Mahāyāna and establish Hīnayāna doctrines. He also authored several dozen secular works, criticizing and rejecting the treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, yet there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with great refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (known in Chinese as Tian Jun, "Heavenly Army") who traveled to and from the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya to resolve his doubts and seek instruction. Devasena used his supernatural powers to take him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya, he merely made a long bow and did not prostrate. Devasena said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha's throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? You are about to receive instruction, so why do you not bow down?" Guṇaprabha replied, "Venerable one, your words are indeed a guide. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while the Bodhisattva Maitreya enjoys the bliss of heavenly rewards and is not a member of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva knew that his heart was firmly set on pride and that he was not a vessel capable of hearing the Dharma; Guṇaprabha went back and forth three times, yet could not resolve his doubts. He again requested Devasena (天軍) to go and pay respects once more, but Devasena, loathing his arrogance, treated him with contempt and did not respond. Since Guṇaprabha (德光) did not have his wishes fulfilled, he gave rise to resentment and immediately went to the mountain forests to practice and develop supernatural powers and meditative concentration; however, because his pride was not yet eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.

issues: Guāngguāng (Guṇaprabha) Monastery → 德光伽藍 = Guṇaprabha's (Déguāng) monastery, name garbled; Saṃghabhadra read it and was moved by it → 遂有心焉: set his mind on [refuting] it; *Kośa-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (俱舍雹論) → 俱舍雹論 is the original title, “Hailstorm on the Kośa” (*Kośakarakā*), and changed the title to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-kārikā-śāstra* (順正理論) → 順正理論 = *Nyāyānusāra*: DM gives the original title the later name and the later title a wrong one, garbling the point of the legend (Mizutani: 『倶舎雹論』… 題を改めて『順正理論』; Beal: “kosha like hail” (karaka) … Nyayanusara); Saṃghabhadra is not yet dead, and you, Great Master, have traveled far away → 眾賢未沒，大師遠迹: while Saṃghabhadra was still alive, you, Master, kept away from him
en_revised: Three or four li to the north of Guṇaprabha's (德光) monastery, there is a large monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. This is the place where the master of treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) passed away. The master of treatises was a man from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). He was intelligent, erudite, and widely learned, and from his youth, he was renowned for his elegance. He delved particularly deeply into the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (說一切有部毘婆沙論) of the Sarvāstivāda school. At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親), who focused his mind on the profound Way and sought to understand the meaning beyond the words. To refute the doctrines held by the Vibhāṣā masters, he composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), which was skillful in its language and meaning, and sublime in its reasoning. Saṃghabhadra read it and set his mind on [refuting] it. Thereupon, he immersed himself in study and rigorous inquiry for twelve years, composing the *Kośakarakā-śāstra* (俱舍雹論, “Hailstorm on the Kośa”) in twenty-five thousand verses, totaling eight hundred thousand words. It is said that his words were profound and his reasoning far-reaching, exhausting the hidden and penetrating the subtle. He told his disciples, "With my outstanding talent and by upholding my correct arguments, go and refute Vasubandhu to blunt his sharp edge, so that the old man may no longer enjoy a monopoly on pre-eminent fame." Thereupon, three or four of his most talented disciples took the treatise he had written and went to seek out Vasubandhu. At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城) in the country of Takka (磔迦國). News spread from afar that Saṃghabhadra was coming. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu immediately began to pack his belongings. His disciples were suspicious and came forward to remonstrate, saying, "The Master’s virtue is higher than that of the ancient sages, and your fame dominates the present age; students from near and far all defer to you. Now, upon hearing of Saṃghabhadra, why are you so flustered? If you must lower yourself, we will be deeply ashamed." Vasubandhu said, "I am traveling far away now, not to avoid this person. It is just that in this country, there are no longer any discerning scholars. Saṃghabhadra is a junior, yet his sophistry flows like a river; I am old and decrepit, and no longer able to engage in debate. I wish to collapse his heterodox views with a single word and lead him to Central India, to face the eminent and learned scholars, so that they may discern truth from falsehood and examine right from wrong." He immediately ordered his companions to pack their book-satchels and set out on the long journey.  Master Saṃghabhadra arrived at this monastery one day later. Suddenly feeling his vitality failing, he composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu, saying: "Since the Tathāgata passed into extinction, the disciples have formed sects, each transmitting their own school’s teachings, each specializing in their own tradition, favoring those of their own path and detesting those of different sects. Being ignorant and of shallow learning, I humbly received the traditional teachings. Having read the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論) composed by you, which refutes the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters, I overreached my abilities and spent many years in deep research to compose this treatise to uphold the orthodox school. My wisdom was small but my ambition was great; now my death is imminent. You, Bodhisattva, expound the subtle words and propagate the supreme truth; if you do not disparage my convictions and allow my writings to be preserved, I shall be fortunate indeed, and what regret could I have in death?"  Thereupon, he selected from among his disciples one who was eloquent and told him: "I am truly a junior scholar who has lightly insulted a senior master; such is my fate, what can be done? I am about to pass away. You must take this letter and the treatise I have composed, apologize to that Bodhisattva, and repent for my transgressions on my behalf." As soon as he finished giving these instructions, he suddenly passed away. The disciple took the letter and went to the place of Vasubandhu (世親), where he delivered the message, saying: "My master, Saṃghabhadra (眾賢), has already abandoned his life. He left instructions to send this letter, to reproach himself and apologize for his faults. That his name not be forgotten is more than we dare hope for." The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu read the letter and examined the treatise; after pondering for a long time, he said to the disciple: "The master of treatises, Saṃghabhadra, was a brilliant junior scholar; though his reasoning was insufficient, his rhetoric was more than enough. I could now refute Saṃghabhadra’s treatise as easily as pointing to the palm of my hand. However, considering his deathbed entrustment and respecting his words acknowledging the difficulty of his task, I shall, for the sake of great righteousness, preserve his lifelong ambition—especially since this treatise actually elucidates my own school of thought." He then changed its title to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論). The disciple remonstrated, saying: "While Saṃghabhadra was still alive, you, Great Master, kept far away from him. Having obtained his treatise, you now change its title; how will all his students have the face to bear such shame?" The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to dispel all doubts, spoke a verse: "Like a lion king, avoiding a pig and going far away; the wise should know the victory or defeat of the two powers."

issues: two hundred paces → 二百餘步: more than two hundred paces
en_revised: After Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) died, his corpse was cremated and his bones were collected; in a mango grove (菴沒羅林) more than two hundred paces northwest of the monastery (伽藍), a stūpa was erected, which still exists today.

issues: Vimalamitra (Tang translation: "Friend of the Stainless," *Wugouyou*) → 無垢友 = “Stainless Friend”; Chinese transcription 毘末羅蜜多羅 not given
en_revised: Beside the Āmra forest is a stūpa containing the remains of the śāstrin Vimalamitra (毘末羅蜜多羅; in Chinese, *Wugouyou*, "Stainless Friend"). The śāstrin was a man of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) who renounced the world in the Sarvāstivāda school. He was broadly versed in the various scriptures and studied heterodox treatises. He traveled through the five Indias, studied the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka, and having established his reputation and completed his work, he prepared to return to his native country. Passing by the stūpa of the śāstrin Saṃghabhadra, he patted it and sighed, saying: "Only you, Master, possessed such noble magnanimity and refined character, expounding the great principles; just as you were about to defeat the heterodox sects and establish the legacy of our own school, why was your life not prolonged! I, Vimalamitra, though a lowly student of the later generation, have long admired your righteousness and cherished your virtue across the ages. Although Vasubandhu has passed away, his school of learning is still transmitted. I shall exhaust all my knowledge to compose various treatises, causing the students of Jambudvīpa to cease praising the Mahāyāna and to extinguish the name of Vasubandhu. This would be an immortal achievement, fulfilling my long-held intention."  Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth. Knowing that his life was surely coming to an end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying: "The Mahāyāna teaching is the ultimate discourse within the Buddha-dharma. Its names and meanings are profound and absolute, and its principles are subtle and mysterious. Because of my ignorance, I lightly refuted the ancients; the karmic retribution is clear, and it is fitting that my body should be destroyed. I dare to warn students: take this as a mirror, each of you be cautious in your intentions, and do not harbor doubts." The great earth shook, and he then expired. At the place where he died, the ground sank into a pit. His traveling companions cremated his corpse, collected the remains, and erected a memorial. At that time, an Arhat (阿羅漢) saw this and sighed, saying, "How regrettable! How painful! This master of treatises (論師), following his own inclinations and clinging to his views, slandered and disparaged the Great Vehicle (大乘), and has fallen into the Uninterrupted Hell (無間獄)."

en_revised: Within the palace city are old foundations, which are the main hall of King Śuddhodana (淨飯王). A *vihāra* (精舍) has been built upon it, inside of which is a statue of the king. Not far to the side are old foundations, which are the bedchamber of Queen Mahāmāyā (摩訶摩耶; Tang language: Great Illusion) (大術). A *vihāra* has been built upon it, inside of which is a statue of the queen. The *vihāra* to the side is the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya descended into his mother’s womb, and inside is a representation of the Bodhisattva’s descent.

issues: shall realize the three bodhis (三菩提) → 三菩提 = *saṃbodhi*, perfect enlightenment, not “three bodhis”
en_revised: To the northeast of the place where the Bodhisattva’s spirit descended, there is a stūpa at the site where the rishi Asita (阿私多) read the prince’s physiognomy. On the day the Bodhisattva was born, auspicious signs converged. At that time, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) summoned the various physiognomists and said to them: "This child has been born; what is his fortune, good or evil? You must examine him thoroughly and speak clearly in your reply." They said: "According to the records of the ancient sages and examining the auspicious omens, if he remains in household life, he will become a Cakravartin (轉輪聖王); if he renounces the household, he will surely attain Samyak-saṃbodhi (等正覺)." At that time, the rishi Asita came from afar and knocked at the gate, requesting an audience. The king was greatly delighted; he personally welcomed him with respect, invited him to a precious seat, and said: "I did not expect that you, Great Seer, would condescend to visit today." The seer said: "While I was dwelling in peace and sitting at ease in the heavenly palace, I suddenly saw hosts of devas dancing. I then asked them, 'Why are you so extremely joyful?' They replied, 'Great Seer, you should know that the first lady of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan in Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) has now given birth to a prince, who shall realize *saṃbodhi* (三菩提) and perfectly illuminate all-encompassing wisdom.' Having heard these words, I have come to pay my respects. What I grieve is that I am old and decrepit, and will not encounter his holy transformation."

issues: A hare arrived later → 蹇兔: a lame hare; the epithet matters, the lame hare is Subhadra in 06.04.x2 (Mizutani: 跛の兎; Beal: a worn-out hare)
en_revised: Not far from the side of the place where the pheasant saved the fire, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, saved lives as a deer. In the remote past, there was a great forest here. A fire broke out in the wilderness, and the flying and running creatures were driven to desperation; facing the peril of a swift current in front and the hardship of a raging fire behind, there were none who did not drown or lose their lives. The deer, moved by compassion, positioned its body across the current, its skin torn and bones broken, exerting itself to rescue the drowning. A lame hare arrived later, and the deer, enduring fatigue and suffering, helped it across. Once its strength was exhausted, it drowned and died. The various devas gathered its remains and erected a stūpa.

issues: Subhadra (in Tang language: Good and Virtuous; the old translation, Subhadra, is incorrect) → the note says the old transcription 須跋陀羅 (Xubatuoluo) is wrong, and Gautama (the old translation, Gautama, is an abbreviated error) → the old form 瞿曇 (Qutan) is erroneous and abbreviated; DM repeats the Sanskrit as the faulted form; transcription 蘇跋陀羅 missing
en_revised: Not far to the west of the place where the deer was rescued from drowning, there is a stūpa. This is the place where Subhadra (蘇跋陀羅; in Chinese, Good and Virtuous; the old form Xubatuoluo 須跋陀羅 is erroneous) entered into extinction. This Good and Virtuous one was originally a master of the Brahmins. He was one hundred and twenty years old, an elder of great wisdom. Hearing that the Buddha was about to enter extinction, he went to the twin trees and asked Ānanda, "The Buddha, the World-honored One, is about to enter extinction. I have doubts and hesitations, and I wish to ask him questions." Ānanda said, "The Buddha is about to enter nirvāṇa; please do not disturb him." He replied, "I have heard that it is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world and difficult to hear the true Dharma. I have deep doubts and fear that I will have no one to ask." Good and Virtuous then entered and first asked the Buddha, "There are various other groups who call themselves teachers, each having different doctrines, handing down instructions to guide the laity. Can Gautama (喬答摩; the old form Qutan 瞿曇 is erroneous and abbreviated) know them all?" The Buddha said, "I have thoroughly investigated them all," and then he expounded them for him. Having heard this, Good and Virtuous had a purified mind and clear understanding; he sought to enter the Dharma and receive the full ordination. The Tathāgata said to him, "Are you truly able to do so? For those of other paths and different schools who wish to practice the holy life, they must be tested for four years. By observing their conduct and examining their nature, if their deportment is tranquil and their speech is truthful, then they may practice the holy life in my Dharma. It depends on the person's conduct; how could this be difficult!" Good and Virtuous said, "The World-honored One is compassionate and merciful, saving and benefiting without partiality. As for the four-year probationary study, my three actions will be in accordance." The Buddha said, "As I have said before, it simply depends on a person's own practice!" Thereupon Subhadra (善賢) left the home-life and received full ordination, diligently applying himself to cultivation with a courageous body and mind. Soon he had no doubts regarding the Dharma and personally attained realization. Before the night was far spent, he attained the fruit of an arhat; his outflows were exhausted and the holy life was established. Unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter the great mahāparinirvāṇa, he entered the samādhi of the fire element (tejo-dhātu-samādhi) amidst the assembly, manifested supernatural powers, and entered extinction first. He was the Tathāgata’s last disciple, yet he entered extinction first; he was the lame hare (蹇兔) who was the last to be ferried across in a former life.

en_revised: To the north of the old palace is a large stone chamber; from the outside it appears like a high mountain, and inside it is several *zhang* wide. It was built by King Aśoka (無憂王) for his younger brother who had left home to become a monk, by employing spirits and ghosts. Originally, King Aśoka had a younger brother by the same mother named Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅; in the language of Tang, "Great Emperor"). Born into the nobility, he wore clothing that usurped royal regulations and was extravagant, indulgent, and violent, causing the populace to harbor resentment. The senior ministers of the state exhorted the king, saying, "Your arrogant brother’s abuse of power has indeed become excessive. When government is equitable, the state is well-ordered; when the people are harmonious, the ruler is secure. This is an ancient teaching that has existed for a long time. We pray you uphold the national laws and hand him over to the law enforcement officials."  King Aśoka said to his brother with tears, "I have inherited the foundation of the ancestors and provide shelter to all living beings; as you are my own flesh and blood, how could I ever forget my kindness and love for you! But because I did not guide you earlier, you have already fallen into the trap of the penal code. Above, I fear the ancestral spirits; below, I am pressured by the public consensus." Mahendra bowed his head and apologized, saying, "I was not prudent in my conduct and dared to violate the national laws; I pray you grant me a new lease on life by allowing a seven-day respite."  Thereupon, he was placed in a secluded chamber and guarded strictly, with fine delicacies and superior food served to him without fail. The guard would call out, "One day has passed; six days remain." By the end of the sixth day, having become deeply fearful and anxious, he exerted his body and mind, attained the fruit of realization, ascended into the void, and manifested miraculous signs. He then departed from the mundane world and dwelt far away in the rocky valleys. King Aśoka went to him in person and said, "Formerly, I was bound by the laws of the state and wished to impose a severe punishment." "How unexpected that you have ascended to purity and attained the holy fruit. Now that you are without attachments or burdens, you may return to the kingdom." The younger brother said, "Formerly I was bound by the net of desire, my mind racing after sounds and forms; now that I have escaped the city of perils, my will finds joy in the mountains and valleys. I wish to abandon the human world and dwell forever among the hills and ravines." The king said, "To quiet the mind and thoughts, is it necessary to seek a secluded cliff? I will follow your wishes and build a retreat for you." He then summoned the spirits and deities and told them, "On a coming day I shall prepare a grand feast of delicacies; you shall lead one another to gather at my assembly, each bringing a large stone to serve as your own seat." The spirits and deities received the order and, when the time arrived, they all gathered. When the assembly had ended, the king said to the spirits, "The stone seats are scattered about; you should stack them up yourselves. With little effort, pile them into a hollow chamber." The spirits and deities received the order and completed it in no time. King Aśoka (無憂王) went in person to welcome and invite him to dwell in this mountain hut.

issues: The two hundred disciples of Gayā-Kāśyapa (伽耶迦葉波), hearing that their brother had abandoned his former practice → 伽耶迦葉波二百門人。聞其兄之捨法也: Gayā-Kāśyapa, with his two hundred disciples, hearing that his brothers had given up their practice, also came; DM makes the disciples the subject and drops Gayā-Kāśyapa's own conversion (Mizutani: 伽耶迦葉波とその二百人の門人は…かれも仏の所へやって来て)
en_revised: Beside the place where the miraculous transformation was manifested, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Tathāgata converted the three brothers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (優樓頻螺迦葉波) and their one thousand disciples. As the Tathāgata was bestowing the Good Path and subduing them according to their needs, the five hundred disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa requested to receive the Buddha’s teachings. Kāśyapa said, "I shall also return from the path of delusion along with you." Thereupon, they followed him and came to the place of the Buddha. The Tathāgata told them, "Discard your deer-skin garments and abandon your fire-worship implements." At that time, the Brahmins respectfully accepted the holy teaching and cast their ritual items into the Nairañjanā River. Nadī-Kāśyapa (捺地迦葉波), seeing the sacrificial utensils drifting away on the current, waited with his disciples for news of his elder brother; when they saw that he had changed his path, they also adopted the dyed robes. Gayā-Kāśyapa (伽耶迦葉波), with his two hundred disciples, hearing that his brothers had abandoned their former practice, also came to the place of the Buddha and wished to practice the holy life.

issues: According to the local customs → 聞諸土俗曰: I heard from the local people; (Original note: pronounced *hàn-suō*, meaning "wild goose" in the language of Tang) → the note 許贈反 is a fanqie reading for 亘 alone, and 唐言雁 = “in Chinese, goose”; DM's pronunciation is invented
en_revised: On the eastern peak there is a monastery. I heard from the local people that the monks there sometimes see, during the night, lamps and torches constantly shining as illumination before the Buddha image in the stone chamber on the western peak. In front of the monastery on the eastern peak of the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (因陀羅勢羅窶訶山), there is a stūpa called Haṃsa (亘娑; 亘 read 許贈反; in Chinese, "wild goose"). Formerly, this monastery studied and practiced the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which is the gradual teaching; therefore, it permitted the consumption of the three pure meats, and this monastery followed this practice without fail. Later, the three pure meats were not always obtainable. A bhikṣu was walking in meditation when he suddenly saw a flock of geese flying by and said in jest, "Today the monks do not have enough for their midday meal; the Mahāsattva should know that now is the time." Before his voice had ceased, one goose flew back, landed in front of the monk, and cast its body down, dying on the spot. When the bhikṣu saw this, he reported the details to the assembly of monks. Those who heard were moved to sorrow and all said to one another, "The Tathāgata established the Dharma to guide beings according to their capacities; we, clinging to our ignorance, have followed the gradual teaching. The Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is the correct principle; we should change our former attachments and strive to follow the holy intent. This goose has offered a warning and is truly a clear guide; we should honor its great virtue and record it for all time." Thereupon, they built a stūpa to manifest its legacy and buried the dead goose beneath it.
